title: Egress connectivity playbook journal
body:
Purpose: personal runbook-style journal while triaging an intermittent egress failure from a private deployment (VPC peering + onprem appliance). Goal is to capture breadcrumbs, commands, outputs, hypotheses and next steps so we can reproduce / hand off to SRE.

Context:
- Private deployment customer (region: us-west-2) using VPC peering to route egress through customer-managed firewall appliance in peered VPC. Redwood control plane in a separate account. Observed: frequent TLS handshake failures for outbound calls to external model repository and some SaaS integrations (webhooks). Failures appear correlated with NAT rotation events on appliance and occasional DNS NXDOMAINs for resolved service names.
- Short timeline: started ~2024-11-10 after network/infra change on customer side (appliance firmware bump). Intermittent (5-15% of requests) for last 48 hours.

Observed behavior & high-level hypothesis:
- Symptoms: connection resets during TLS ClientHello -> server aborts with TCP RST or TLS handshake timeout. Some connections succeed after retry.
- DNS: occasional NXDOMAIN or long lookup latency (~300-600ms) from nodes. When DNS misses, clients sometimes fall back to cached IPs and succeed.
- Hypothesis A: appliance or peering path is doing transient packet drops or reordering causing TLS timeouts on long RTT path. Hypothesis B: MTU/MSS clamping or PMTU blackhole causing TLS ClientHello with SNI+ALPN (larger) to be fragmented/dropped. Hypothesis C: DNS proxy on appliance returns SERVFAIL intermittently.

Evidence gathered so far (commands and outputs):
- From a node in customer VPC (k8s pod) to external repo (example: models.example.net):
  curl -v https://models.example.net/api/status --connect-timeout 5
  Output snippet (one of failing attempts):
  "*   Trying 52.23.11.7:443...
* TCP_NODELAY set
* Connection timed out after 5001 milliseconds
* Closing connection 0
curl: (28) Connection timed out after 5001 milliseconds"

- Same pod, tcpdump capture during failure window (pcap saved to /tmp/pcap-1119.pcap). Quick tcpdump filter used:
  sudo tcpdump -nni eth0 host 52.23.11.7 and port 443 -w /tmp/pcap-1119.pcap
  Observations in pcap (wireshark): repeated SYN retransmits, then occasional RST after SACKs. Sequence shows SYN -> SYN+ACK sometimes arrives but subsequent packets lost.

- MTU probe from pod to endpoint:
  ping -M do -s 1400 52.23.11.7
  Output: "Message too long" on some attempts, other attempts succeed. Suggests inconsistent PMTU handling or ICMP being rate-limited/dropped through appliance.

- DNS query latency and SERVFAILs from node resolver:
  time dig +tries=2 +time=2 models.example.net @10.0.0.2
  ;; -> SERVFAIL (10% attempts) ; average 220ms; sometimes NXDOMAIN while upstream resolves fine from other networks.

- Logs from customer appliance (provided by oncall): shows lines of "dns-proxy: dropped query for udp 53 from 10.20.x.x due to rate-limit" and "conntrack: delete stale entry, src=10.20.x.x dst=52.23.11.7 sport=49152 dport=443" around same timestamps.

Quick root-cause candidates:
- Conntrack table eviction causing mid-flow state loss; short-lived TCP flows get reset when appliance deletes conntrack entry.
- DNS proxy rate-limiting causes fallback to IPv6 or legacy IPs that are filtered / blackholed by peering route.
- PMTU blackhole due to blocked ICMP fragmentation-needed messages across peering path; larger TLS ClientHello packets get dropped.

Immediate reproduction steps performed:
1) Reproduced with a simple stress script from pod (small load):
   for i in {1..100}; do curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}\n" https://models.example.net/api/status; done
   Result: ~12% failures with timeout or connection reset.
2) Ran pcap during run and correlated failing requests to missing three-way handshake or RST after handshake.
3) Ran dig in a loop to watch DNS behavior: noted spikes of SERVFAIL from 10.0.0.2 resolver corresponding to failure windows.

Commands tried to mitigate / test:
- Reduced concurrent connection rate (application side) -> failure rate dropped to ~6% (supports conntrack exhaustion angle).
- Forced small MSS/MTU on pod veth to 1200 to avoid fragmentation -> failure rate dropped to 1-2% for same experiment.
  ip link set dev eth0 mtu 1200 (in container netns)
- Switched pod DNS to external resolver (8.8.8.8) via /etc/resolv.conf override (quick test) -> DNS SERVFAILs disappeared and immediate success rate rose; but not acceptable as long-term.
- Enabled TCP keepalive and longer retransmit windows in client -> small improvement, but not root fix.

Notes from logs/metrics:
- Conntrack usage on appliance peaked at 65% during baseline load but shows sharp transient spikes up to 98%; when spike occurs, appliance starts aggressive cleanup.
- Customer firewall has default conntrack timeout for ESTABLISHED 432000s but maximum conntrack table size low (32k). Short bursts of ephemeral ports exhausted table.

Actionable next steps (short-term):
- Recommend customer increase conntrack table size and tune timeouts / enable hashsize autoscale if supported. (Ticketed with customer infra ops.)
- Suggest enabling PMTU discovery / allow ICMP type 3 code 4 (fragmentation needed) across peering path and appliance; verify ICMP is not dropped by intermediate firewall.
- Add DNS caching closer to pods (dns-autoscaler / CoreDNS tuning) to reduce queries to appliance DNS proxy.
- As temporary mitigation, lower pod MTU to 1200 or enable MSS clamping on appliance to avoid fragmentation.

Follow-up experiments to run:
- Controlled test with iperf3 across peering during failure window to reproduce packet loss/reordering patterns.
- Reproduce with tcpdump on both sides (pod and appliance external-facing interface) to determine where packets are dropped.
- Run tracepath/traceroute -M to detect PMTU and where ICMP message is lost.
- Simulate conntrack exhaustion by opening many ephemeral outgoing connections from a test node while capturing appliance conntrack behavior.

Hand-off notes (what to tell SRE/customer ops):
- Provide pcap /dig logs and timestamps (pcap: /tmp/pcap-1119.pcap, dig-run-1119.log)
- Include a short summary of correlation between conntrack spikes and TLS failures; point to appliance logs with rate-limit and conntrack delete entries.
- Recommended immediate mitigation: increase conntrack size, enable MSS clamping, and allow ICMP fragmentation-needed messages.

Unresolved questions / open items:
- Why are conntrack spikes happening for HTTP/HTTPS outbound flows? Is there a burst pattern from some internal agent (sidecar?) that opens many short-lived connections? Need to correlate application traces.
- Confirm whether peering NAT translation preserves path MTU ICMP messages back to the originating pod (some peers do not forward ICMP TTL exceeded/fragments).
- Is there any intermediate NAT gateway on Redwood side that might be rewriting ports aggressively and causing conntrack collisions?

Log pointers and filenames (local):
- /var/log/rdw/egress/debug-2024-11-19.log (curl attempts, timestamps)
- /tmp/pcap-1119.pcap (tcpdump from pod)
- /tmp/dig-run-1119.log (dig loop output)
- /mnt/customer/appliance/logs/dns-proxy-1119.log (provided by customer)

If we don't get a config change from customer quickly, plan to:
- Instrument more telemetry in workload: connection latencies, per-ip failure counts, and correlate with pod restarts; add alert if >5% failures over 5m.
- Provide temporary documented workaround (MTU=1200 or client-side backoff) and a small k8s job to apply node-level MTU where supported.

Final quick notes to self:
- Keep pcap and dig logs zipped and attach to JIRA-5172.
- Ask Jin to run concurrent conntrack stress test in staging peered VPC tomorrow morning (coordinate 09:00 PST).
- Follow up with customer to get appliance firmware changelog and any ACL change log around 2024-11-10.

-- Asha
